speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked the Minister for Education whether the Ministry tracks the career impact of SkillsFuture credits on Singaporeans who have utilised them in terms of (i) employment status (ii) hours worked and (iii) wage outcomes, since such data may increase take-up rates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what is the rationale for restricting the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance to citizens aged 40 years and above since skills obsolescence affects all ages; (b) whether the Ministry will consider the reskilling needs of workers in their 30s; and (c) whether the Ministry will expand SkillsFuture to support postgraduate qualifications (i) in critical sectors or (ii) in general.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Industry-relevant training programmes are subsidised at up to 70% of the course fees for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At age 25, Singaporeans receive $500 in SkillsFuture Credit, which they can use to develop their skills and interests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For Singaporeans who are 40 and above, they can use the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme (SFLP).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This programme helps them to pursue a substantive skills reboot and helps them stay competitive in a rapidly changing economy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are prioritising support for our mid-career Singaporeans, as they may face higher risk of skills obsolescence, having completed their original work-ready qualifications many years ago.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At this stage in life, given their heavy family and work responsibilities, they also face higher opportunity costs in pursuing upskilling and reskilling, particularly when they take up substantive courses that require greater time and financial commitment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If they choose to pursue substantive training, the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme helps them lower the opportunity cost in two ways.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, by providing further course fee support in the form of the SkillsFuture Credit (Mid-Career) top-up of $4,000.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Introduced in May 2024, individuals can use the Credit to further offset out-of-pocket training costs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is over and above course fee subsidies of up to 90%.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, we provide financial support for those pursuing longer substantive training, such as full qualifications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance helps to partially offset income loss during full-time training.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, the SkillsFuture Credit (Mid-Career) top-up can be used for over 7,000 courses, of which, about 700 full-time training programmes qualify for training allowance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up courses are carefully curated to support substantive training, with the aim of improving a person's employability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They include full qualifications offered by the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These programmes provide good upgrading pathways that continue to enjoy good wage premium, as our studies have shown.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Individuals looking to transition into another sector can consider SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes that provide training for up to 12 months as well as employment facilitation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Between June 2022 when the Programme started and December 2024, about 55% of almost 4,300 SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme trainees who were previously unemployed found new jobs within six months after course completion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As of July 2025, there are about 330 SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes offered in 21 sectors with good hiring opportunities such as Information and Communications, Professional Services and Food Services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The take-up of the Level-Up Programme has been positive.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: From the claims data, the number of individuals taking SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes increased by about six times from around 1,500 to around 8,500, compared to the same period in the preceding year, and those who used the SkillsFuture Credit for full qualifications increased by about 2.5 times from around 3,000 to around 7,000.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To build on this momentum, we will expand the Level-Up Programme in the following ways for the immediate term.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, as announced at Budget 2025, we will expand the training allowance to part-time long-form training from early next year, to support mid-career Singaporeans who choose to pursue such training while continuing to work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is estimated to benefit 10,000 Singaporeans annually.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, we will continue to refresh and expand the number of IHL full qualifications and stackable micro-credentials, as well as SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes to meet emerging skills needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, over 100 SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes were launched this year in high-demand areas such as Artificial Intelligence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Third, we will work with sector agencies and industry partners to include more courses offered by industry leaders and private training providers that are well-recognised by industry and confer credentials that lead to strong employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to monitor the training needs of adult learners over their life stages as we expand the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In particular, let me respond to two suggestions that Members have raised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, on extending the Level-Up Programme to younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For now, younger Singaporeans in their 30s can continue to benefit from the broad-based training support that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This includes subsidies at up to 70% of course fees for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Additional support will be given to lower-wage workers in their 30s.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Earlier this year, the Ministry of Manpower announced the Workfare Skills Support Level-Up Programme to better support these workers in upgrading to full qualifications that can uplift their wages.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: From early 2026, lower-wage workers in their 30s will receive monthly training allowance when they pursue eligible long-form training, similar to the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The second suggestion is to extend the training allowance to postgraduate programmes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are also careful not to inadvertently perpetuate a paper chase at the Masters’ level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Individuals can decide whether it is worthwhile to invest in a Masters’ degree, given its high cost but also potentially high returns on investment, however, this applies to a small number of jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to monitor the needs for postgraduate training in emerging sectors and adjust our level of support accordingly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We welcome feedback and will continue to monitor the employment outcomes from the increased training take-up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The success of the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme ultimately must be measured by how confident mid-career Singaporeans are in using their newly acquired skills to navigate the disruptions in the economy ahead, and cannot just be measured by employment outcomes alone, since training alone cannot guarantee jobs and may not lead to immediate employment gains.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To help our people succeed, we need to continue strengthening the whole-of-society partnerships between Government, individuals, unions, industry and training institutions to build a culture of lifelong learning so Singaporeans can stay resilient, employable and competitive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My question to the Senior Minister of State is, what can we do, or can employers do more?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And how can we get them to better support both, from the employer-supported aspect as well as the individual-initiated training, as we embrace SkillsFuture in the next lap?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, we would ask for employers to do more to support our SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And overall, if you take a look at the last 10 years, the numbers have indeed increased.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have seen an increase in the number of employers that are involved and an increase in the number of training places supported by employers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But as the overall number of training places has increased, the proportion has remained relatively static.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We think there is room for the proportion to increase and for employers to do more.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is also a benefit for the system and our movement, if employers can do more.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because if they are sending their workers for training, it means that they have recognised and are signalling the importance of such skills upgrading for their business and for their industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It means that their workers and the learners under SkillsFuture have the assurance that these are industry relevant and are going to help them progress in their career.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And it helps to, then embed this culture of lifelong learning as part of adult work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of it is about the business decisions and the sense of investment in their people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And some of it is also looking at the processes within their companies, in terms of reducing the frictions to allow people to go for training, have the work covered and think about the job transformation that will allow the embedding of lifelong learning as part of the career.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think there is room for the employers to do more.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of it is about decisions in terms of the returns on investment that they will have and some of it is about reducing the frictions for their workers as learners in pursuing lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Senior Minister of State about the learnings that we have, given the fact that this is new programme and it is attracting a different group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I note in particular the statistics of around more than 50% of people who are able to get a job after this training.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Is there any preliminary sense of what happens to the rest?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am asking because these groups are perfectly motivated people – they have a full-time job and then they transit, they retrain and, therefore, they should logically be able to get such skills because they highly motivated and are employable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, are there any lessons that we can learn or preliminary conclusions, especially with regard to matching the aspirations and qualifications of the trainees with the future industry needs?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is an important issue, but it is a little bit preliminary, it is a little bit premature.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The programme is not very old and some of the types of gains that he is talking about will indeed take years to be realised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You transition into a new industry or even stay within the industry but now with the new set of qualifications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Although you have the qualifications, you now have to apply them to the job, develop your career prospects within this new role in this new task.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The better we can do that, the more confidence the employers will have in the approach that we are taking and hence, the more confidence that workers and learners will have in dealing with the opportunity cost that is very real for someone undergoing training.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, those are some of the short-term lessons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think the issues that the Member has highlighted are indeed important, but it is a little bit early to have a definitive comment on that.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I understand and appreciate the reasons why 40 was used as an age cut-off for the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am just wondering whether the Ministry has data on the appeals put to the Ministry for those aged 40 and below for the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance – because studying those data may show us how better we can support the age group beyond just SkillsFuture itself.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, the decision to think of the age cut-off at 40 is informed by data, but not so much on the data that we have on appeals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not have the direct data for appeals received or granted.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Perhaps the Member can return with a further question, if that is the focus.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The data that informs us about the age cut-off is about the risks of a given individual becoming unemployed, and the length of time taken for that individual to then go back into the workforce and find a job.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And we can see that those in their 40s have a higher risk of becoming unemployed, potentially because of skills obsolescence, and take longer to then go back into the workforce and to find employment, as compared to people in their 20s and 30s.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so for that reason, we have chosen the cut-off for that particular tier to be at 40.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I just want to take the opportunity to emphasise that it does not mean that anybody under the age of 30 does not have assistance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are the subsidies that are available to all Singaporeans at up to 70%, potentially rising to 90% if it is employer-driven; there is the SkillsFuture Credit that is available to everybody above the age of 25; and the moves that we are making to support lower-wage workers that are above the age of 30 that are coming and have already been announced.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would also point out that there are plenty of training opportunities available to Singaporeans of all ages that are not under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The public sector is one, for example, that provides training through the Civil Service College and so public sector officers do not have to use the SkillsFuture Credit in order to develop new opportunities through training.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And there are many other employers that are doing something similar.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the second question is in regards to the clause restricting the Mid Career Training Allowance to undergraduate qualifications.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: On Monday, Deputy Prime Minister Gan said that there were five growth areas: precision medicine, AI, green economy, autonomous vehicles, space, and there is a strong research and development (R&D) and reskilling component for all of these industries.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For those that have reliable data that I have managed to find, most of the R&D jobs – 90% to 100% of them – do require postgraduate degrees; and generally, in the industry, it appears that 30% to 40% of the jobs in the industry do require postgraduate degrees.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I will just ask the Senior Minister of State, does he not agree that the clause restricting postgraduate qualifications does not really align with the spirit of the Ministry of Trade and Industry's future strategy?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For his first question on the age cut-off and the training participation, I think that we should not take the view that what we must strive for is for everyone to use up their SkillsFuture Credit as soon as possible, and to engage in training as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The idea is to make sure that there is an assurance that at any time of your career over the course of your life, you will have the opportunity to reskill should there be a need.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, if there is no need – you are within a career, you are developing your professional skillsets, there is opportunity ahead of you – then, that may be the right thing for you to do, rather than using your SkillsFuture Credit and going for a course for a certification.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want you to get into the culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so perhaps, if there is an interest, a small course, please do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I think we should not necessarily see the data in a negative light.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It may well be that that category of people does not need to utilise the SkillsFuture Credit in quite the same way and may need to do so at a future point in their career – which is its purpose.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the second point in terms of the postgraduate support, as I have explained, we are open to considering if there is a need.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue is whether today, the supply of people with appropriate qualifications in order to drive the development of those areas is constrained by the type of training that is provided.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not appear to be a direct indication at this point in time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We would also not want, as we are developing these programmes, to create a paper chase.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Certainly, we do not want people to go and chase after postgraduate qualifications if they are not going to result in outcomes for that individual, which are useful to that individual.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will learn from the lessons as we implement it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And should the need be there, we can always consider it again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first part of my question actually was about the utilisation of SkillsFuture credits generally.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, taking the Senior Minister of State's point that SkillsFuture is meant for the long term, does the Senior Minister of State see this as a problem and is this something for which, say, the expiry should be extended, or something for which we should encourage people to utilise more quickly?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would encourage all Members of this House who I am sure are in the eligible age group, please do use up your expiring credits by the end of the year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But that is not the end of the SkillsFuture Credit, and there is the additional $500 opening Credit and then the $4,000 that is available for the long term which does not expire.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want to encourage people to take a few courses; and for some of the courses, you do not need to use very much of your SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Get into the habit of understanding what does lifelong learning look like and what does it mean to take a course while you are working if you have not done something like this before.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is worth having your first taste of what it feels like to do lifelong learning and make use of those credits to do a course.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I must remind myself and my constituents this weekend.
